title: Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinematics

1.3 Linear motion: equations of motion and their graphical treatment
1.4 Projectile motion, with and without a resistive force

html:
This chapter is the toolkit of the whole Physics paper: units and dimensions, significant figures and errors, vectors, and the description of straight-line and projectile motion.

The Mechanics area carries 10 of the 50 Physics questions , with about 2 questions from this chapter.

They are usually quick marks — a dimensional formula, a significant-figure count, an angle between two vectors, a reading from a velocity–time graph, or a projectile range — and the same skills are needed silently in every later chapter.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Dimensional formulae of common quantities, and which pairs share dimensions.
  • Using dimensions: checking an equation, converting units, finding the dimensions of a constant.
  • Counting significant figures; rounding a sum or product correctly; percentage error of A^pB^q/C^r.
  • Resultant of two vectors, R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta, and its special cases (0°, 90°, 120°, 180°).
  • Dot and cross products: angle between vectors, perpendicular and parallel tests, area of a parallelogram.
  • Equations of motion, the distance in the nth second, and reading slopes and areas of motion graphs.
  • Projectile formulas T, H, R; complementary angles; horizontal projection; what air resistance changes.

1.1 Precision, accuracy, significant figures and dimensional analysis

Units and base quantities

A physical quantity is anything that can be measured; it is written as a number times a unit. The SI system has seven base (fundamental) quantities; every other quantity is derived from them.

Base quantity SI unit Symbol Dimension
Length metre m [L]
Mass kilogram kg [M]
Time second s [T]
Electric current ampere A [A] (or [I])
Thermodynamic temperature kelvin K [K] (or [Θ])
Amount of substance mole mol [mol] (or [N])
Luminous intensity candela cd [cd] (or [J])

Plane angle (radian) and solid angle (steradian) are dimensionless.

Accuracy, precision and errors

Accuracy and precision

Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another (and, for an instrument, how fine its smallest reading — its least count — is).

A set of readings can be precise but inaccurate (tightly grouped around the wrong value — typical of a systematic error such as a zero error), or accurate on average but imprecise (scattered around the true value — typical of random errors).

Error type Cause Reduced by
Systematic zero error, faulty calibration, a fixed habit of the observer, ignored air drag correcting the instrument or the method; not by repeating
Random unpredictable small fluctuations taking many readings and averaging
Gross (blunder) misreading, wrong recording care; rejecting the odd reading

For readings a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n with mean \bar a: the absolute error of a reading is |\bar a - a_i|; the mean absolute error \Delta a is the mean of these; relative error = \Delta a/\bar a; percentage error = (\Delta a/\bar a)\times 100\,\%.

Least count (the smallest reading an instrument can make): vernier calliper LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = (value of 1 MSD)/(number of vernier divisions), when n VSD coincide with (n-1) MSD; screw gauge LC = pitch / number of circular-scale divisions.

A metre rule has LC 1 mm, a typical vernier 0.1 mm, a typical screw gauge 0.01 mm.

Combining errors

Result Maximum error
Z = A + B or Z = A - B \Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B (absolute errors add)
Z = AB or Z = A/B \frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = \frac{\Delta A}{A} + \frac{\Delta B}{B} (relative errors add)
Z = A^n \frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = n\frac{\Delta A}{A}
Z = \frac{A^pB^q}{C^r} \%Z = p(\%A) + q(\%B) + r(\%C)
Errors never subtract

Even when a quantity is divided or appears with a negative power, its percentage error is added. In Z = A^2/B^3 the percentage error is 2(\%A) + 3(\%B), not 2(\%A) - 3(\%B).

And a subtraction A - B of two nearly equal numbers has a large percentage error even if each reading is good.

Worked example 1.1 — error in g from a pendulum

Problem. In g = 4\pi^2 l/T^2 the length l is measured with an error of 2 % and the period T with an error of 1 %. Find the maximum percentage error in g.

Solution. 4\pi^2 is exact. \%g = 1\times(\%l) + 2\times(\%T) = 2 + 2(1) = 4\,\%. The power of T doubles its share — measure T (time many oscillations) most carefully.

Significant figures

The significant figures (SF) of a measured value are the reliably known digits plus the first uncertain one.

Rule Example SF
All non-zero digits count 4.256 4
Zeros between non-zero digits count 4.005 4
Leading zeros never count (they only fix the decimal point) 0.00420 3
Trailing zeros after a decimal point count 4.200 4
Trailing zeros of a whole number without a decimal point are ambiguous 4200 2, 3 or 4
The power of ten does not count 6.02 × 10²³ 3

Write 4200 as 4.2 × 10³ (2 SF) or 4.200 × 10³ (4 SF) to remove the doubt. Changing units does not change the number of significant figures: 2.30 m = 230 cm = 2.30 × 10⁻³ km — always 3 SF (230 cm is better written 2.30 × 10² cm).

Arithmetic.

  • Addition and subtraction: keep as many decimal places as the number with the fewest decimal places. 12.1 + 0.25 + 1.256 = 13.606 → 13.6.
  • Multiplication and division: keep as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest SF. 2.5 × 1.25 = 3.125 → 3.1.
  • Rounding: drop a digit below 5 (2.743 → 2.74); raise the previous digit if the dropped digit is above 5 (2.746 → 2.75). When the dropped digit is exactly 5, the common convention keeps the previous digit if it is even and raises it if it is odd (2.745 → 2.74, 2.735 → 2.74).

Dimensions and dimensional analysis

The dimensions of a quantity are the powers to which the base quantities must be raised to represent it; the expression is its dimensional formula. Force = ma has [M][LT^{-2}] = [MLT^{-2}].

Quantity From Dimensional formula SI unit
Force ma [MLT^{-2}] N
Work, energy, torque Fs, rF [ML^2T^{-2}] J, N m
Power W/t [ML^2T^{-3}] W
Momentum, impulse mv, Ft [MLT^{-1}] kg m s⁻¹, N s
Pressure, stress, elastic modulus, energy density F/A [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] Pa
Surface tension, spring constant F/l, F/x [MT^{-2}] N m⁻¹
Coefficient of viscosity F/(A\,dv/dx) [ML^{-1}T^{-1}] Pa s
Gravitational constant G Fr^2/(m_1m_2) [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}] N m² kg⁻²
Planck's constant, angular momentum E/f, mvr [ML^2T^{-1}] J s
Moment of inertia mr^2 [ML^2] kg m²
Frequency, angular velocity, velocity gradient 1/T, \theta/t [T^{-1}] Hz, rad s⁻¹
Specific heat capacity Q/(m\Delta T) [L^2T^{-2}K^{-1}] J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
Latent heat Q/m [L^2T^{-2}] J kg⁻¹
Stefan's constant \sigma P/(AT^4) [MT^{-3}K^{-4}] W m⁻² K⁻⁴
Charge It [AT] C
Potential difference W/q [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}] V
Resistance V/I [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}] Ω
Magnetic field B F/(qv) [MT^{-2}A^{-1}] T

Dimensionless quantities: strain, angle, refractive index, relative density, coefficient of friction, Poisson's ratio, Reynolds number. (Angle has a unit, the radian, but no dimensions.)

Principle of homogeneity

Every term on both sides of a correct physical equation has the same dimensions. Only quantities of the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated, and the argument of \sin, \cos, e^x or \log must be dimensionless.

Uses.

  1. Checking an equation: s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 — each term is [L], so it is dimensionally correct (correctness of the \frac{1}{2} is not tested).
  2. Dimensions of a constant: in v = at + \frac{b}{t+c}, c is added to t so c = [T]; b/t is a velocity, so b = [LT^{-1}][T] = [L].
  3. Converting units: a quantity with dimensions [M^aL^bT^c] has numerical values related by n_2 = n_1\left(\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right)^a\left(\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right)^b\left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^c. For example 1 J = 1\times(10^3\ \text{g/g})(10^2\ \text{cm/cm})^2 = 10^7 erg.
  4. Deriving a relation when a quantity is a product of powers of others.
Worked example 1.2 — deriving a formula

Problem. The speed v of a transverse wave on a string depends on the tension F and the mass per unit length \mu. Find the form of the relation.

Solution. Put v = kF^x\mu^y: [LT^{-1}] = [MLT^{-2}]^x[ML^{-1}]^y. Matching powers: M: 0 = x + y; L: 1 = x - y; T: -1 = -2x. So x = \frac{1}{2}, y = -\frac{1}{2} and v = k\sqrt{F/\mu} (experiment gives k = 1).

Limitations. Dimensional analysis cannot find dimensionless constants (\frac{1}{2}, 2\pi); cannot handle relations containing sums of different terms, or trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions; cannot, in mechanics, find a relation with more than three unknown powers (only three equations, from M, L, T); and cannot tell apart quantities with the same dimensions (work and torque).

Fast dimension work in the paper

Memorise five anchors — force [MLT^{-2}], energy [ML^2T^{-2}], pressure [ML^{-1}T^{-2}], charge [AT], voltage [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}] — and build the rest by one division or multiplication.

To compare options, check one base quantity at a time (often the power of T alone eliminates three options).

1.2 Scalars and vectors: laws of addition, resolution, scalar and vector products

A scalar has magnitude only (mass, time, work, energy, power, pressure, temperature, charge, electric current, potential).

A vector has magnitude and direction and obeys the laws of vector addition (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, impulse, torque, electric field).

Electric current has a direction but adds algebraically at a junction, so it is a scalar; finite rotations do not add like vectors either.

Addition of vectors

  • Triangle law: place \vec B with its tail at the head of \vec A; the resultant runs from the tail of \vec A to the head of \vec B.
  • Parallelogram law: if \vec A and \vec B are the adjacent sides from one point, the diagonal from that point is \vec R = \vec A + \vec B.
  • Polygon law: for many vectors joined head to tail, the closing side (tail of the first to head of the last) is the resultant. If they form a closed polygon, the resultant is zero.

For two vectors at angle \theta, the resultant's magnitude and its angle \alpha with \vec A are

R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}, \qquad \tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}

Angle \theta Resultant R
0° (parallel) A + B (maximum)
90° \sqrt{A^2+B^2}
180° (antiparallel) |A - B| (minimum)
any \theta, with A = B 2A\cos(\theta/2)
120°, with A = B A

So |A - B| \le R \le A + B: forces of 3 N and 5 N can give any resultant from 2 N to 8 N, but not 1 N or 9 N. Subtraction is adding the reverse vector: |\vec A - \vec B| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 - 2AB\cos\theta}. Vector addition is commutative and associative.

Worked example 1.3 — resultant of two forces

Problem. Forces of 3 N and 4 N act at a point with 60° between them. Find the resultant.

Solution. R = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 2(3)(4)\cos 60^{\circ}} = \sqrt{37} = 6.1\ \text{N}.

Check against the limits it must lie between 1 N and 7 N, and above 5 N (the 90° value) because the angle is less than 90°.

Zero resultant

Two vectors give zero only if they are equal and opposite. Three coplanar vectors can give zero (they close a triangle) — e.g. 3 N, 4 N, 5 N — but 2 N, 3 N and 6 N cannot, because 6 > 2 + 3.

Three vectors that are not in one plane can never add to zero; at least four are needed.

Resolution and unit vectors

A vector \vec A at angle \theta to the x-axis has rectangular components A_x = A\cos\theta and A_y = A\sin\theta, so A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2} and \tan\theta = A_y/A_x.

In three dimensions, \vec A = A_x\hat i + A_y\hat j + A_z\hat k and |\vec A| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}. The unit vector along \vec A is \hat A = \vec A/|\vec A|.

The direction cosines satisfy \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1. A component can be zero but never larger than the vector itself.

Scalar (dot) and vector (cross) products

Scalar product \vec A\cdot\vec B Vector product \vec A\times\vec B
Definition AB\cos\theta (a scalar) AB\sin\theta\,\hat n, \hat n by the right-hand rule
In components A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z (A_yB_z - A_zB_y)\hat i + (A_zB_x - A_xB_z)\hat j + (A_xB_y - A_yB_x)\hat k
Order commutative: \vec A\cdot\vec B = \vec B\cdot\vec A anticommutative: \vec A\times\vec B = -\vec B\times\vec A
Unit vectors \hat i\cdot\hat i = 1, \hat i\cdot\hat j = 0 \hat i\times\hat j = \hat k, \hat j\times\hat k = \hat i, \hat k\times\hat i = \hat j, \hat i\times\hat i = 0
Zero when \theta = 90^{\circ} (perpendicular) \theta = 0^{\circ} or 180^{\circ} (parallel)
Physics W = \vec F\cdot\vec s, P = \vec F\cdot\vec v, flux = \vec B\cdot\vec A \vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F, \vec L = \vec r\times\vec p, \vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B
Geometry projection of \vec A on \vec B = \vec A\cdot\vec B/B area of parallelogram = |\vec A\times\vec B|; triangle = \frac{1}{2}|\vec A\times\vec B|

The angle between two vectors: \cos\theta = \frac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{AB}. \vec A\times\vec B is perpendicular to both \vec A and \vec B.

Worked example 1.4 — angle between two vectors

Problem. Find the angle between \vec A = \hat i + \hat j and \vec B = \hat j + \hat k.

Solution. \vec A\cdot\vec B = (1)(0) + (1)(1) + (0)(1) = 1 and A = B = \sqrt{2}. So \cos\theta = 1/2 and \theta = 60^{\circ}.

Three one-line tests

|\vec A + \vec B| = |\vec A - \vec B| means \vec A\perp\vec B. \vec A\cdot\vec B = |\vec A\times\vec B| means \theta = 45^{\circ}. \vec A\cdot\vec B = 0 means perpendicular; \vec A\times\vec B = 0 means parallel (for components, A_x/B_x = A_y/B_y = A_z/B_z).

1.3 Linear motion: equations of motion and their graphical treatment

Distance (path length, scalar) is never less than the magnitude of displacement (vector, straight line from start to end). Average speed = total distance / total time; average velocity = total displacement / total time.

Instantaneous velocity v = dx/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2 = v\,dv/dx.

Equations of uniformly accelerated motion

For constant acceleration a, initial velocity u, final velocity v, displacement s in time t:

v = u + at, \qquad s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2, \qquad v^2 = u^2 + 2as

s = \frac{(u+v)}{2}\,t, \qquad s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)

s_n is the displacement in the nth second (its unit is metre; the "per second" is hidden in the 1 s interval). They hold only if a is constant.

Fast fact (from rest, uniform a) Ratio
Distances in successive equal intervals (1st, 2nd, 3rd second) 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 (Galileo's odd numbers)
Total distances after 1, 2, 3 s 1 : 4 : 9 (s\propto t^2)
Velocities after 1, 2, 3 s 1 : 2 : 3
Stopping distance for the same braking s \propto u^2 — double the speed, four times the distance

Average speed for two halves. Equal distances at v_1 and v_2: \bar v = \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2} (harmonic mean). Equal times: \bar v = \frac{v_1+v_2}{2}.

Free fall (air resistance neglected) is uniform acceleration g downward. Dropped from rest: h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2, v = \sqrt{2gh}.

Thrown up at u: maximum height H = u^2/2g, time up = u/g = time down, total time 2u/g, and it returns with the same speed u. All bodies fall with the same g in vacuum, whatever their mass.

Relative velocity on a line: v_{AB} = v_A - v_B. Cars moving the same way at 60 and 40 km h⁻¹ close at 20 km h⁻¹; moving towards each other, at 100 km h⁻¹.

Motion graphs

Graph Slope gives Area under it gives
Position–time (x–t) velocity —
Velocity–time (v–t) acceleration displacement (area above axis +, below −); total area ignoring sign = distance
Acceleration–time (a–t) rate of change of acceleration change in velocity
Motion x–t graph v–t graph
At rest horizontal line on the time axis
Uniform velocity straight sloping line horizontal line
Uniform acceleration parabola, curving upward straight line, positive slope
Uniform retardation parabola, curving downward straight line, negative slope
Ball thrown up and caught (up positive) inverted parabola straight line of slope -g crossing the axis at the top

A v–t graph can never be vertical (infinite acceleration) and an x–t graph can never turn back in time (a body cannot be at two places at once).

Worked example 1.5 — the last-second trick

Problem. A stone dropped from rest covers 25 m in the last second of its fall (g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}). From what height was it dropped?

Solution. In the nth second, s_n = \frac{g}{2}(2n-1) = 5(2n-1) = 25, so n = 3: the fall lasts 3 s. Height h = \frac{1}{2} g t^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10)(9) = 45\ \text{m}.

Signs in vertical motion

Choose one direction as positive and keep it. With "up" positive, a = -g on the way up and on the way down; at the top v = 0 but a = -g still.

A body thrown down from a height and one thrown up with the same speed reach the ground with the same speed (energy), but at different times.

1.4 Projectile motion, with and without a resistive force

A projectile is a body thrown into the air and then acted on by gravity alone (no air resistance). Its motion is two independent motions: uniform velocity horizontally (a_x = 0) and free fall vertically (a_y = -g).

For launch speed u at angle \theta above the horizontal on level ground: u_x = u\cos\theta (constant throughout), u_y = u\sin\theta.

Quantity Formula
Time of flight T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}
Maximum height H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}
Horizontal range R = \frac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}, maximum R_{max} = \frac{u^2}{g} at \theta = 45^{\circ}
Path (trajectory) y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta} = x\tan\theta\left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right) — a parabola
Velocity at time t v_x = u\cos\theta, v_y = u\sin\theta - gt, v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}
At the highest point v = u\cos\theta (horizontal), a = g downward, KE = K\cos^2\theta
Range and height R = 4H\cot\theta, so \tan\theta = 4H/R; at 45°, H = R/4
Change in momentum, launch to landing 2mu\sin\theta, vertically downward

Complementary angles. \theta and 90^{\circ} - \theta give the same range (15° and 75°, 30° and 60°), but different heights and times; for them H_1 + H_2 = u^2/2g, T_1T_2 = 2R/g and R = 4\sqrt{H_1H_2}.

Worked example 1.6 — oblique projection

Problem. A ball is kicked at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal (g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}). Find T, H and R.

Solution. u_y = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}, u_x = 10\sqrt{3} = 17.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}. T = 2u_y/g = 2\ \text{s}; H = u_y^2/2g = 100/20 = 5\ \text{m}; R = u_xT = 34.6\ \text{m} (or u^2\sin60^{\circ}/g = 20\sqrt{3}).

Horizontal projection

A body thrown horizontally at speed u from height h: u_y = 0, so the time to fall t = \sqrt{2h/g} is the same as for a body simply dropped from that height.

Horizontal distance x = u\sqrt{2h/g}; path y = \frac{gx^2}{2u^2} (measured downward); striking speed v = \sqrt{u^2 + 2gh}, at angle \tan\phi = \sqrt{2gh}/u below the horizontal.

Worked example 1.7 — relief drop

Problem. A helicopter flying horizontally at 50 m s⁻¹, 490 m above flat ground near Jumla, releases a relief packet (g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}, no air resistance). How far ahead of the release point does it land?

Solution. t = \sqrt{2(490)/9.8} = \sqrt{100} = 10\ \text{s}; x = 50\times10 = 500\ \text{m}. The packet stays vertically below the helicopter all the way down — both have the same horizontal velocity.

With a resistive force (air drag)

Real air exerts a drag force opposite to the velocity, roughly F = kv at low speeds and F \propto v^2 at high speeds. This changes the results above:

Without air resistance With air resistance
Horizontal velocity constant Horizontal velocity keeps decreasing
Path a symmetric parabola Path not a parabola; the descending branch is steeper than the rising one
Time up = time down Time up less than time down (drag adds to g on the way up and subtracts from it on the way down)
Lands with the launch speed Lands with a smaller speed (energy lost to the air)
Maximum range at 45° Range and height both reduced; maximum range at an angle below 45°

Terminal velocity. A body falling through a fluid speeds up until the drag (plus buoyancy) equals its weight; then the net force is zero and it falls at a constant terminal velocity.

For drag kv, mg = kv_t gives v_t = mg/k, and the velocity grows as v = v_t(1 - e^{-kt/m}), reaching about 63 % of v_t after one time constant m/k.

Raindrops and parachutists fall at terminal velocity; Stokes' law for a sphere in a viscous fluid (Chapter 4) is the same idea.

What does not change at the top

At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, but the speed is u\cos\theta, not zero, and the acceleration is still g downward. Only a body thrown straight up (\theta = 90^{\circ}) is momentarily at rest at the top.

Worked example — killing wrong options with dimensions

A formula is offered for the period of a pendulum in four forms: T = 2π√(l/g), T = 2π√(g/l), T = 2π√(ml/g), T = 2π(l/g). Which survive a dimension check?

  • Dimensions: [l] = L, [g] = LT⁻², so l/g has dimensions T² and √(l/g) has dimension T ✓.
  • √(g/l) has dimension T⁻¹ ✗ (that is a frequency).
  • √(ml/g) contains M½T ✗ — a period cannot depend on mass this way.
  • (l/g) alone has dimension T² ✗.

Only T = 2π√(l/g) can be correct — and you never needed the derivation. Note the limit of the method: it cannot verify dimensionless constants (the 2π) and cannot distinguish quantities with identical dimensions, like torque and energy.

Trap — significant figures in multiplication

2.4 × 1.35 = 3.24 on a calculator, but the answer may carry only two significant figures (that of 2.4): 3.2.

The rule: multiplication/division follows the fewest significant figures; addition/subtraction follows the fewest decimal places. Examiners place 3.24 and 3.2 side by side precisely to catch this.

Formula and fact sheet

Topic Formula or fact
Least count vernier: 1 MSD − 1 VSD; screw gauge: pitch / circular divisions
Errors Z = A\pm B: \Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B; Z = A^pB^q/C^r: \%Z = p\%A + q\%B + r\%C
SF in + / - fewest decimal places
SF in \times / \div fewest significant figures
Unit conversion n_2 = n_1(M_1/M_2)^a(L_1/L_2)^b(T_1/T_2)^c
Same dimensions work = energy = torque [ML^2T^{-2}]; momentum = impulse [MLT^{-1}]; pressure = stress = modulus = energy density [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]; h = angular momentum [ML^2T^{-1}]; surface tension = spring constant [MT^{-2}]
Resultant R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta; \tan\alpha = B\sin\theta/(A + B\cos\theta); equal vectors: R = 2A\cos(\theta/2)
Dot product AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z; zero for perpendicular
Cross product AB\sin\theta; zero for parallel; \hat i\times\hat j = \hat k; area of parallelogram = |\vec A\times\vec B|
Equations of motion v = u + at; s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as; s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1)
Free fall v = \sqrt{2gh}; thrown up: H = u^2/2g, T = 2u/g
Average speed, equal distances 2v_1v_2/(v_1+v_2)
Projectile T = 2u\sin\theta/g; H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g; R = u^2\sin2\theta/g; R_{max} = u^2/g
Projectile extras R = 4H\cot\theta; \theta and 90^{\circ} - \theta same R; KE at top = K\cos^2\theta
Horizontal projection t = \sqrt{2h/g}; x = u\sqrt{2h/g}; v = \sqrt{u^2 + 2gh}
Linear drag v_t = mg/k; with drag, time up < time down, range smaller, best angle < 45°

Chapter summary

  • Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings. Systematic errors spoil accuracy and are not removed by repeating.
  • Leading zeros never count as significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point do. Sums keep the fewest decimal places, products the fewest significant figures.
  • Percentage errors always add, each multiplied by its power: \%(A^pB^q/C^r) = p\%A + q\%B + r\%C.
  • Every term in a correct equation has the same dimensions; dimensions convert units and derive power-law relations, but cannot give numerical constants or tell work from torque.
  • R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta; |A - B| \le R \le A + B; two equal vectors at 120° have a resultant equal to either.
  • \vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta (zero when perpendicular), |\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta (zero when parallel, equals the parallelogram area).
  • v = u + at, s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1); slope of v–t = acceleration, area = displacement.
  • Projectile: T = 2u\sin\theta/g, H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g, R = u^2\sin2\theta/g; maximum range at 45°; complementary angles give equal ranges.
  • Air resistance lowers and shortens the path, makes the fall slower than the rise, and moves the best angle below 45°; a falling body reaches terminal velocity when drag balances weight.

Practice questions

Set A — Recall (20 questions)

  1. The dimensional formula of Planck's constant isa[ML²T⁻²]b[ML²T⁻¹]c[MLT⁻¹]d[ML²T⁻³]
  2. The number of significant figures in 0.003060 isa2b3c4d7

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Derive the time of flight, maximum height and range of a projectile and solve a numerical. [10]
  2. Explain dimensional analysis, its uses and limitations, and combine errors in a measurement. [10]

Model answer D1: projectile motion (10 marks)

Introduction. A projectile is a body thrown into the air that then moves under gravity alone. Air resistance is ignored. Its path is a parabola because the horizontal motion is uniform and the vertical motion is uniformly accelerated.

Derivation. Let the speed of projection be u at an angle \theta above the horizontal. The components are u_x = u\cos\theta and u_y = u\sin\theta.

  1. Time of flight. The body returns to ground level when y = 0: 0 = (u\sin\theta)T - \tfrac12 gT^2, so T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}.
  2. Maximum height. At the top v_y = 0, so 0 = u^2\sin^2\theta - 2gH and H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}.
  3. Range. The horizontal distance is R = u_xT = u\cos\theta\cdot\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}.
  4. Equation of path. Eliminating t from x = u\cos\theta\,t and y = u\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac12gt^2 gives y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}, a parabola.
  5. Maximum range. R is greatest when \sin2\theta = 1, that is \theta = 45^{\circ}, and then R_{max} = u^2/g. Angles \theta and 90^{\circ}-\theta give the same range, and H = R\tan\theta/4.
Quantity Formula Depends on
Time of flight T 2u\sin\theta/g u, \theta, g
Maximum height H u^2\sin^2\theta/2g u, \theta, g
Range R u^2\sin2\theta/g u, \theta, g
Speed at top u\cos\theta u, \theta only

Numerical. A ball is thrown at 50\ \text{m s}^{-1} at 37^{\circ} (\sin37^{\circ} = 0.6, \cos37^{\circ} = 0.8, g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}).

Then T = 2(50)(0.6)/10 = 6\ \text{s}, H = (30)^2/20 = 45\ \text{m} and R = 40 \times 6 = 240\ \text{m}. The speed at the top is 40\ \text{m s}^{-1}, purely horizontal.

Conclusion. The two components are independent. Time and height depend on u\sin\theta, range on u^2\sin 2\theta, and the maximum range is at 45^{\circ}.

Model answer D2: dimensional analysis and combination of errors (10 marks)

Introduction. The dimensions of a quantity show how it depends on the base quantities mass [M], length [L] and time [T]. Dimensional analysis uses the rule that every term in a physical equation must have the same dimensions (the principle of homogeneity).

Uses.

  1. Checking an equation. For s = ut + \tfrac12at^2, each term has dimension [L], so the equation is dimensionally correct.
  2. Converting units. n_2 = n_1\left[\dfrac{M_1}{M_2}\right]^a\left[\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^b\left[\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right]^c. For example 1\ \text{N} = 10^5 dyne.
  3. Deriving a relation. For a pendulum, assume T = k\,l^xm^yg^z. Matching [T] gives y = 0, x = \tfrac12, z = -\tfrac12, so T = k\sqrt{l/g} (with k = 2\pi found by experiment).

Limitations. It cannot find dimensionless constants such as \tfrac12 or 2\pi.

It fails for relations containing sums of terms, trigonometric, logarithmic or exponential functions, and it cannot decide whether a quantity is a scalar or a vector. A dimensionally correct equation need not be physically correct.

Combination of errors.

Operation Rule
Z = A + B or A - B \Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B (absolute errors add)
Z = AB or A/B \dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z} = \dfrac{\Delta A}{A} + \dfrac{\Delta B}{B}
Z = A^nB^m \dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z} = n\dfrac{\Delta A}{A} + m\dfrac{\Delta B}{B}

Numerical. In a pendulum experiment l = 100.0 \pm 0.1\ \text{cm} and T = 2.00 \pm 0.02\ \text{s}. From g = 4\pi^2l/T^2, \dfrac{\Delta g}{g} = \dfrac{0.1}{100} + 2\left(\dfrac{0.02}{2.00}\right) = 0.001 + 0.020 = 0.021, which is 2.1\%.

Also g = 4\pi^2(1.000)/4.00 = 9.87\ \text{m s}^{-2}, so \Delta g = 0.21\ \text{m s}^{-2} and g = 9.87 \pm 0.21\ \text{m s}^{-2}.

Conclusion. Dimensional analysis checks and guides an equation but never proves it. In experiments the quantity with the highest power or the biggest percentage error (here T) controls the final accuracy.
